lessons.title: Meet the three goal types
lessons.body:
Goal setting is about creating a clear target for what you want to work toward. 

There are three types of goals:  
• Learning goals focus on learning something or preparing for a behaviour. 
• Performance goals focus on doing a behaviour at a certain frequency, time, or amount. 
• Outcome goals focus on a result you want to work toward.  

Let’s try a short example to make the difference clearer.

lessons.title: A performance goal
lessons.body: Here’s an example:  “I will go to the yoga studio twice per week, on Mondays and Wednesdays.”  What type of goal is this?
lessons.hint: Not quite — take another look at what the goal is focusing on.  Is it mainly about learning something, doing a behaviour at a specific frequency or amount, or working toward a result?
lessons.feedback: Exactly — that is a Performance goal because it focuses on doing a behaviour at a specific frequency and on specific days.

lessons.title: A learning goal
lessons.body: Here’s another example:  “I want to learn which exercises would be safe and suitable for me before I begin.”  What type of goal is this?
lessons.hint: Not quite — look again at what the person is trying to do.  Are they mainly trying to learn or prepare, carry out a behaviour at a certain frequency or amount, or work toward a result?  Choose the option that fits best.
lessons.feedback: Exactly — that is a Learning goal because it focuses on learning or gathering information that can help prepare someone for the behaviour.

lessons.title: An outcome goal
lessons.body: Here’s one final example:  “I want to improve my cardiovascular fitness so that I can complete a 5 km walk more comfortably.”  What type of goal is this?
lessons.hint: Not quite — focus on the end result the person is hoping to achieve.  Is the goal mainly about learning something, doing a behaviour at a specific frequency or amount, or working toward a result?  Choose the option that fits best.
lessons.feedback: Exactly — that is an Outcome goal because it focuses on a result the person wants to work toward.

practice.title: Choose your goal type
practice.body: Learning goals build knowledge or skills. Performance goals focus on doing a behaviour. Outcome goals focus on a result.
practice.question: Which type fits what you want to work toward?

practice.title: Your goal
practice.body: Choose something that fits your own circumstances.
practice.question: What goal can I help you with today?

practice.title: What matters to you
practice.body: Your reasons can help you decide whether this goal fits.
practice.question: Why is this goal meaningful to you?

practice.title: Check your confidence
practice.body: A smaller step is a useful place to begin.
practice.question: How confident do you feel about working toward this goal?

practice.title: Make it doable
practice.body: Think about energy, accessibility, time, and available support. You can revise the draft before saving.
practice.question: What makes this goal realistic for you, or what would you adjust?

title: Action Planning & Problem Solving
subtitle: Turn your goal into a flexible plan

lessons.title: Make a clear plan
lessons.body:
Action Planning helps you turn a physical activity goal into a specific plan by deciding what you will do, when you will do it, where you will do it, and how you will carry it out. 

Problem Solving helps you think ahead about things that might get in the way of your plan and decide what you could do if those barriers happen. 

Together, they can help make your goal easier to put into practice.  

Would you like to see an example, or go straight to making your own plan?

lessons.title: The details that help
lessons.body: Here are two ways someone could plan for the same physical activity goal:  Plan A: “I’ll try to walk more this week.”  Plan B: “I’ll walk around my neighborhood for 30 minutes on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday at 6 PM.”  Which one is the clearer action plan?
lessons.hint: Not quite — think about which plan gives the person clearer details about what they will do, when they will do it, where they will do it, and how they will carry it out.  Which plan is the clearer action plan?
lessons.feedback: Exactly — Plan B is the clearer action plan because it specifies what the person will do, when they will do it, where they will do it, and how long they will do it for.

lessons.title: Prepare for a barrier
lessons.body: Let’s build on the walking plan from the previous example.  The person plans to walk around their neighborhood for 30 minutes on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday at 6 PM.  They realize that bad weather might make it difficult to walk outside.  Which response is the clearer Problem Solving plan?  Plan A: “I’ll just hope the weather is good.”  Plan B: “If the weather is bad on a walking day, then I will walk indoors at the mall.”
lessons.hint: Not quite — think about which response actually prepares the person for the barrier instead of leaving it to chance.  Which option gives them a clear plan for what they will do if bad weather gets in the way?
lessons.feedback: Exactly — Plan B is the clearer Problem Solving plan because it identifies what the person will do if the barrier happens. The if/then format makes the response to the barrier specific and easier to act on.

practice.title: What will you do?
practice.body: We’ll build on your confirmed goal.
practice.question: What activity or preparation step will you do?

practice.title: Choose a time
practice.body: A time or cue can make a plan easier to remember.
practice.question: When will you do it?

practice.title: Choose a place
practice.body: Consider where the plan is accessible and practical.
practice.question: Where will you do it?

practice.title: Work out the details
practice.body: Consider duration, equipment, support, or how you will get started.
practice.question: How will you carry it out?

practice.title: Think ahead
practice.body: Plans can change when circumstances change.
practice.question: What might get in the way?

practice.title: Your if/then plan
practice.body: Prepare an alternative that fits the barrier you identified.
practice.question: If that happens, what will you do instead?

practice.title: Choose a reminder
practice.body: Use a cue that fits into your day.
practice.question: What could remind you to use this plan?

lessons.title: Track what is useful
lessons.body:
Self-Monitoring means keeping track of something that can help you understand your physical activity or your progress toward being more physically active. 

What you monitor can depend on where you are right now. If you are mainly thinking about or preparing for physical activity, you might track something useful during that preparation. If you are already being physically active, you might track something about the activity itself. 

A Self-Monitoring plan usually includes what you will track, how you will record it, when you will record it, and how often. 

Would you like to see an example, or go straight to making your own Self-Monitoring plan?

lessons.title: Choose a manageable method
lessons.body: Here are two ways someone could keep track of their physical activity:  Plan A: “I’ll try to remember how active I was.”  Plan B: “After each planned walk, I’ll write in my phone note whether I completed it.”  Which one is the clearer Self-Monitoring plan?
lessons.hint: Not quite — think about which plan clearly states what the person will keep track of and how they will record it, rather than relying on memory alone.  Which one is the clearer Self-Monitoring plan?
lessons.feedback: Exactly — Plan B is the clearer Self-Monitoring plan because it specifies what the person will track, how they will record it, and when they will record it.

practice.title: Where are you now?
practice.body: Tracking can support preparing for activity as well as doing it.
practice.question: Which stage fits you right now?

practice.title: Choose what to notice
practice.body: Track something useful to you, without adding unnecessary burden.
practice.question: What will you track?

practice.title: Choose a method
practice.body: A note, checklist, or short reflection may fit.
practice.question: How will you record it?

practice.title: Choose when
practice.body: Connect recording to a moment that works for you.
practice.question: When will you record it?

practice.title: Choose a review rhythm
practice.body: Reviewing can help you understand what is working.
practice.question: How often will you review what you recorded?

title: Talking to Yourself About Physical Activity
subtitle: Positive self-talk, self-praise, and positive re-framing

lessons.title: Three skills for talking to yourself
lessons.body: This guide introduces Positive Self-Talk, Self-Praise, and Positive Re-framing. Notice how the words you use about physical activity affect your motivation.

lessons.title: Positive self-talk
lessons.body: Motivational self-talk can support confidence, mood, and effort. Instructional self-talk focuses on how to perform an activity. Choose statements that feel positive, freely chosen, and motivating to you; saying them aloud may help.

lessons.title: Self-praise
lessons.body: Self-praise recognizes progress or rewards effort in physical activity. You can choose a statement that acknowledges what you have done and when you would like to use it.

lessons.title: Positive re-framing
lessons.body: Notice all-or-nothing thinking, mental filtering, catastrophizing, or emotional reasoning. Identify the thought, consider evidence for and against it, and build a more balanced thought.

lessons.title: Reflect on what helps
lessons.body: After trying self-talk, self-praise, or positive re-framing, reflect on what was useful and whether it affected your engagement in physical activity.

practice.title: Choose your self-talk
practice.body: Choose a phrase that fits you. You may choose motivational or instructional self-talk.
practice.question: What positive self-talk statement would you like to use?

practice.title: Type of self-talk
practice.body: Motivational supports confidence, mood, or effort; instructional focuses on the process of an activity.
practice.question: Would you describe it as motivational or instructional?

practice.title: Use your statement
practice.body: Consider when this statement is useful and how often to repeat it.
practice.question: When and how often would you like to use it?

practice.title: Self-praise
practice.body: Choose words that recognize effort or progress.
practice.question: What would you like to tell yourself after making progress?

practice.title: Notice a difficult thought
practice.body: You can also practise positive re-framing.
practice.question: What difficult thought about physical activity would you like to work through?

practice.title: Check the evidence
practice.body: Think about evidence for and against your thought.
practice.question: What evidence supports or challenges that thought?

practice.title: Find a balanced thought
practice.body: A re-framed thought can be realistic rather than forced positivity.
practice.question: What balanced thought fits the evidence?
